How to use this page

  • It shows the form. Each draft follows the course template and is written to the rubric, so you can see what a complete section looks like.
  • It is not an answer key. Your organization, model and data are your own, so copy the habits and not the content.
  • Its model gets tested. The current version is careful work, and careful work can still rest on a model that turns out to be incomplete. When the evidence calls for a revision, the revision is posted with what was learned and why.
  • Every number comes from the posted data. Download the file and check any of them with Gemini.

What version 1 taught us version 2

Version 1 asked whether Fernhill’s July 2025 reorganization raised delivery, and its first analysis (below, under “Earlier: version 1”) couldn’t say. This entry records what that analysis found, what we noticed but set aside, what we decided to do about it and why, and what changed in the project as a result. When a model changes, everything built on it changes too, so version 2 redoes the Project Brief and the Data & Methods draft from the start.

What version 1 found

  • On average delivery was 1.9 points lower in the four quarters after July 2025 (63.4%) than in the eight before (65.3%), a weak difference, since every quarter after sits inside the range of the quarters before.
  • The middle moved the other way. The median team-quarter delivered 72.6% after against 68.2% before, while the most common band stayed at 80% to 90%. The three measures told three stories because the spread widened. The weakest tenth of team-quarters delivered about 35% or less before and about 19% or less after.
  • People-skill ratings rose from 0.69 to 0.79, as the model predicted, while delivery didn’t.
  • Quarters rated hard at close fell from 52.8% to 41.0%, and quarters rated easy rose from 74.9% to 79.4%.

Taken at the average, all three of version 1’s tests failed, and the reorganization looks like a mistake. Taken at the median, delivery rose by about what the model predicted. An average and a median are not two ways of saying the same thing. They agree only when the distribution is symmetric, and this one was not.

Why we didn’t conclude “it failed”

  1. Two changes at once. Professional managers and AI licenses arrived together in every team, 480 team-quarters with both and 960 with neither. In this data they are one variable, so any difference belongs to both, and nothing can split it.
  2. Something else changed at the same moment. Committed work rose 12% in July 2025 with the year’s customer migration. Teams delivered more milestones than before (12.8 a quarter, against 11.6) but a smaller share of a bigger load. Version 1 had assumed nothing else would change, and had chosen not to check.
  3. The hard-quarter test was circular. Difficulty was rated at quarter’s close, after the outcome was known. Quarters that delivered under 60% were rated hard 83% of the time, against 21% of the rest. A rating made afterward can’t separate “hard work went badly” from “work that went badly was called hard.”
  4. No comparison group. Every team changed, so the only baseline was the past, and the past can’t absorb a change that hit the whole firm.

Noticed, not pursued (yet)

The file held records version 1’s model never asked about. - Escalations fell from 9.9 to 7.5 a team-quarter after July 2025, so something changed in where technical questions go, and the model had no place for it. - Lead departures rose from 3.6% to 11.9% of teams a quarter. We read that as churn after a reorganization and set it aside. - The spread widened. The median rose while the average fell because the weakest quarters got weaker (under 10% delivered in 1.2% of team-quarters before and 6.7% after) while the middle improved. We took that for noise in a weak difference and did not ask what was splitting the teams. - We never asked IT what teams actually did. Version 1 wrote that licenses show only access. The same system logs use, and we hadn’t asked for it.

What we decided, and why

Decision Why
Separate the two changes into three groups, engineer-managers without AI, engineer-managers with AI, and professional managers with technical leads and AI Reason 1, so the reorganization and AI can be told apart
Assign the groups by lot, 40 teams each, and compare each group with its own eight quarters before Reasons 2 and 4, since a firm-wide change falls on every group alike, and the lot makes the groups comparable
Rate difficulty at the quarterly planning review, before the work Reason 3, since a rating made before the outcome can’t be bent by it
Ask IT for the usage logs A license says who could use AI, not who did, and a no-AI arm has to stay that way
Model where technical questions go, through escalations and the wait for an answer from whoever holds technical judgment Version 1’s claims that “AI covers the gaps” and “nothing technical is lost” couldn’t be checked against any record, and escalations were moving

Every one of these uses records Fernhill already keeps, including IT licenses (which arrive in waves anyway), IT’s usage logs, the planning tool, the planning review, and the issue tracker.

A note on the data. Fernhill is a simulation, so we can replay the same year at the same firm (the same 120 teams, the same people, the same luck) with the design version 1’s results call for. A real firm gets one try, which is why the design has to come before the data.

Project Brief version 2

Download the PDF The same Brief as a two-page document.

1. The organization

Fernhill Software is a useful fiction, a business-software firm with about 1,100 engineers in 120 product teams. It hires engineers on technical skill and promotes its strongest into management, where some struggle. In 2025, as AI coding tools arrive, an AI enthusiast on the leadership team proposes a three-part reorganization. First, hire professional managers on people skill instead of promoting engineers. Second, make each team’s engineer-manager its technical lead, keeping technical judgment but managing no one. Third, let AI fill the manager’s technical gaps. Fernhill runs a one-year pilot from July 2025, assigning its 120 teams by lot to three arms of 40 so the reorganization and AI can be told apart.

2. The model

A team delivers when two jobs get done, coordinating people and resolving technical unknowns. The proposal splits those jobs between a manager and a lead, with AI assisting both.

  1. People skill lowers coordination friction. Less work sits blocked on other people, more so in bigger teams.
  2. Difficulty sets how many unknowns arrive. AI resolves routine ones but helps little on hard ones.
  3. Escalated unknowns queue at whoever holds technical judgment, the engineer-manager or a tech lead with far more time. Near capacity, the wait explodes (Little’s Law).

In short, AI should help most on easy work, and the new structure most on hard work, where queues form.

For the model to be right, the professional managers must have more people skill than the engineer-managers they replace. Teams must stay in their arm, and teams without AI must go without it. The leads must accept their new role. Difficulty must be judgeable at quarterly planning. What stays unmeasured is the judgment holder’s capacity, which shows only through waits.

3. The question

Should Fernhill replace engineer-managers with professional managers backed by technical leads and AI? The pilot answers with two comparisons, with each arm also set against its own eight pre-pilot quarters. The first compares AI, holding structure fixed (engineer-managers with and without AI). The second compares structure, holding AI fixed (manager + lead vs. engineer-manager, both with AI), the decision Fernhill faces.

4. The prediction

Stated before looking at this version’s data:

  • AI alone raises delivery on easy quarters by about 8 points, and cuts their escalations by about 40%, but changes little on hard quarters.
  • People-skill ratings are higher under professional managers.
  • The new structure shortens escalation waits, most on hard quarters, and on hard quarters delivers about 5 points more than engineer-managers with AI.

The model is wrong if any of these holds:

  • AI’s gain is as large on hard quarters as on easy ones.
  • The new structure’s waits are no shorter on hard quarters.
  • Its waits are shorter but its delivery is no better. Then the queue isn’t what limits delivery.

5. The data sketch

The data. Fernhill’s records have one row per team per quarter, July 2023 to June 2026 (1,440 rows), and they are simulated, since Fernhill is fictional. The variables, by concept. The change is arm (assigned by lot), manager type, and AI licenses, with IT’s usage logs. The manager has a people-skill rating on the eight Project Oxygen behaviors, and the hours work sits blocked on other teams. The work has team size, and difficulty rated at planning (a rating new with the pilot). Unknowns are escalations, and the hours each waits. The outcome is the share of committed milestones delivered on time.

6. The disciplinary anchor

Whom to promote (organizational management). Firms promote their best performers, who then make worse managers (Peter and Hull, 1969; Benson, Li and Shue, 2019). People skill keeps teams together, and Google’s Project Oxygen ranked technical skill last of eight manager behaviors (Hoffman and Tadelis, 2021; Garvin, 2013).

The work itself (operations management). Unknowns go up the hierarchy unless knowledge is cheap, and AI makes only routine knowledge cheap (Galbraith, 1974; Garicano, 2000; Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond, 2025; METR, 2025). Waits grow when escalations arrive faster than they are cleared (Little’s Law).

The method. The pilot is randomized, so the lot makes the arms comparable and their differences are the effects of AI and of the structure.

Note on AI use

I used Gemini (Willamette account) to turn the critique of version 1 into a pilot design and size its arms. It suggested a fourth arm, a professional manager without AI. I rejected it, since three arms answer the decision Fernhill faces. It suggested surveying how managers and leads work together. I left that out, since the escalation wait already measures how fast technical questions get answered.

Data & Methods draft version 2

Download the PDF The same draft as a two-page document, with its charts.

The data behind every number here: fernhill_v2.csv, also in The data below.

1. Unit of observation

One row of my data is one product team in one quarter, because the lot assigns whole teams and delivery is counted by the quarter. There are 1,440 rows, from 120 teams over 12 quarters, July 2023 to June 2026, eight before the pilot and four during it. The lot assigned teams, 40 to an arm, so arm comparisons rest on 40 teams each, not on 480 team-quarters.

2. Variable table

Concept Variable Kind Source What it misses
Structure and AI arm Labels Pilot register Drift from the arm
Before or after period Labels Calendar Half-done quarters
Unknowns escalations Counts Tracker Hallway answers
Waiting esc_wait_hrs Measurement (hours) Tracker Untracked waits
Difficulty hard_plan Yes/No Planning review Misjudged quarters
Delivery delivered_share Measurement (share) Planning tool Customer value and renegotiation

3. Data source

Fernhill’s pilot register, IT licenses, issue tracker, planning review, and planning tool, read through People Analytics, cover all 120 teams for all 12 quarters. The planning review has rated difficulty only since July 2025. A second file from IT logs AI use by team for the four pilot quarters. The main file also holds records my model doesn’t call for (escalations still open at quarter’s close, departures, the lead’s former role). Gemini suggested describing them, and I left them out. I use the usage logs only to check that the no-AI arm stayed off licensed tools. Fernhill is a useful fiction, so these records are simulated, but not from the model above. They come from a model this version doesn’t see, whose units are these team-quarters and whose relationships, noise, and assumptions are published in Module 3. Until then, I treat them as the firm’s records.

4. Quality concern

The difficulty rating at planning is the most likely to mislead. It is mismeasured whenever planners misjudge a quarter, and missing before July 2025, when nobody rated difficulty at planning. If planners misjudge, I would see quarters rated easy with as many escalations as hard ones, which makes the hard–easy difference look smaller. I will split results by the planning rating, never by the close-of-quarter rating made after the outcome, and say that misjudged quarters shrink any difference.

5. First description

Delivery (delivered_share). Kind: a measurement, a share from 0 to 1. How many: 1,440, none blank. Middle: median 0.68, and mean 0.64, which a tail of bad quarters pulls down. Spread: half fall between 0.50 and 0.82, and the range is 0 to 1. Shape: skewed left, with a long tail of quarters that delivered little (24 under 5%). Choice: each team-quarter counts once, whatever its size. Weighting by milestones gives 0.63.

Against my model: not yet able to say, since one variable can’t show whether the arms differ.

Waiting (esc_wait_hrs). Kind: a measurement, in hours. How many: 1,399, with 41 blank (3%). The gaps are in the tracker, before and during the pilot. Middle: median 15.5 hours, and mean 28.6, which a few very long waits pull up. Spread: half fall between 8.4 and 34.7 hours, and the range is 3.2 to 1,382. Shape: skewed far right, with 30 team-quarters waiting over 100 hours, the longest about eight weeks. Choice: blanks left out. Long waits kept, since nothing says they are errors, and the chart stops at 100 hours.

Against my model: consistent so far, since a long right tail is what a queue near capacity produces. Whose waits they are is a comparison for Module 2.

Difficulty (hard_plan). Kind: yes/No. How many: 480, all in the pilot, with 960 blank before July 2025, when the rating didn’t exist. Middle, spread and shape: 0.44 rated hard (210 quarters). With two values, the proportion says it all. Against my model: not yet able to say, but there are enough quarters of each kind to compare the arms on hard and easy work.

Note on AI use

I used Gemini (Willamette account) for the counts, middles, spreads, and histograms. I kept the median for waits, since long waits pull the mean, and rejected its offer to drop waits over 100 hours, since nothing says they are errors.

This is a complete project through its Results draft, with careful, honest work on a model that turned out to be incomplete, and the reason the next version exists. It stays here because we learn from mistakes too.

Project Brief version 1

Download the PDF The same Brief as a two-page document.

1. The organization

Fernhill Software is a useful fiction, a business-software firm with about 1,100 engineers in 120 product teams. It hires engineers on technical skill and promotes its strongest into management, where some struggle. In 2025, as AI coding tools arrive, an AI enthusiast on the leadership team proposes a three-part reorganization. First, hire professional managers on people skill instead of promoting engineers. Second, make each team’s engineer-manager its technical lead, keeping technical judgment but managing no one. Third, let AI fill the manager’s technical gaps. Fernhill adopts the plan in all 120 teams in July 2025, with AI at the same time.

2. The model

A team delivers when two jobs get done, coordinating people and resolving technical unknowns. The proposal splits those jobs between a manager and a lead, with AI assisting both.

  1. People skill lowers coordination friction. Less work sits blocked on other people, more so in bigger teams.
  2. AI covers the manager’s technical gaps. It explains technical status, checks estimates, and drafts plans.
  3. Technical judgment stays with the lead, who resolves the team’s unknowns as the engineer-manager did, so nothing technical is lost.

In short, the reorganization puts people skill in the manager’s chair without losing technical judgment, so delivery rises.

For the model to be right, the professional managers must have more people skill than the engineer-managers they replace. AI must cover the manager’s technical gap on hard work as well as easy. The leads must accept their new role. Nothing else that affects delivery may change at the same time. What stays unmeasured is whether AI actually covers the manager’s gap, since licenses show only access.

3. The question

Should Fernhill replace engineer-managers with professional managers backed by technical leads and AI? The rollout answers with one comparison. It compares before and after July 2025 across all 120 teams, which shows the whole package as adopted, if nothing else changed.

4. The prediction

Stated before looking at this version’s data:

  • Delivery rises after July 2025, by about 5 percentage points, after a dip in the first quarter.
  • People-skill ratings rise after the reorganization.
  • The rise holds on hard quarters as well as easy ones, because AI covers the technical gap.

The model is wrong if any of these holds:

  • Delivery is no higher after the reorganization than before.
  • People-skill ratings rise but delivery doesn’t. Then people skill isn’t what drives delivery.
  • Delivery rises on easy quarters but falls on hard ones. Then AI doesn’t cover the technical gap.

5. The data sketch

The data. Fernhill’s records have one row per team per quarter, July 2023 to June 2026 (1,440 rows), and they are simulated, since Fernhill is fictional. The variables, by concept. The change is before or after July 2025, manager type, and AI licenses. The manager has a people-skill rating on the eight Project Oxygen behaviors, and the hours work sits blocked on other teams. The work has difficulty, rated at the quarter’s close. The outcome is the share of committed milestones delivered on time.

6. The disciplinary anchor

Whom to promote (organizational management). Firms promote their best performers, who then make worse managers (Peter and Hull, 1969; Benson, Li and Shue, 2019). People skill keeps teams together, and Google’s Project Oxygen ranked technical skill last of eight manager behaviors (Hoffman and Tadelis, 2021; Garvin, 2013).

The work itself (operations management). Cheaper knowledge means fewer problems go up the hierarchy, and AI helps less experienced workers most (Garicano, 2000; Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond, 2025).

The method. The comparison is before and after for the whole firm, with eight quarters of history as the baseline.

Note on AI use

I used Gemini (Willamette account) to turn the leadership proposal into relationships and match each concept to a record. It suggested checking for other 2025 changes that could move delivery. I listed that as an assumption, since the customer migration is a workload change, not a management change. It suggested rating difficulty at planning. I rejected that, since the quarter-close review already rates every quarter.

Data & Methods draft version 1

Download the PDF The same draft as a two-page document, with its charts.

About this draft's one weak spot. Scored against the Data & Methods rubric, this draft loses points on the data source. It does not say "These data are simulated from the model described above," and it does not list the relationships, noise and assumptions behind the records. That is deliberate. Its author does not know the model that produced these records, so cannot describe it honestly. Version 3 is where the model and the data finally match, and where that sentence belongs. Adding it here would make this draft say something untrue.

1. Unit of observation

One row of my data is one product team in one quarter, because each team has its own manager and delivery is counted by the quarter. There are 1,440 rows, from 120 teams over 12 quarters, July 2023 to June 2026, eight before the reorganization and four after. All 120 teams changed managers in July 2025, and AI licenses arrived the same month, so manager_type, period and ai_access move together and make one comparison, not three. Each team has its own manager, as the Brief says (the file has no manager ID to check), so a row is also one manager’s quarter, which is what my model is about.

2. Variable table

Concept Variable Kind Source What it misses
Manager type manager_type Labels HR system Skill within a type
Before or after period Labels Calendar Half-done quarters
People skill people_rating Measurement (share) Upward survey Likability and non-response
AI ai_access Yes/No IT licenses Actual use
Difficulty hard_close Yes/No Close review Difficulty seen beforehand
Delivery delivered_share Measurement (share) Planning tool Customer value and renegotiation

3. Data source

Fernhill’s HR system, quarterly upward feedback survey, IT licenses, quarter-close review, and planning tool, read through People Analytics, cover all 120 teams for all 12 quarters. The file also holds records my model doesn’t call for (team size, escalations, waits, departures). Gemini suggested describing them, and I left them out. Fernhill is a useful fiction, so these records are simulated, but not from the model above. They come from a model this version doesn’t see, whose units are these team-quarters and whose relationships, noise, and assumptions are published in Module 3. Until then, I treat them as the firm’s records.

4. Quality concern

The people-skill rating is the most likely to mislead, being a survey answer and not a count. It is missing for 102 of 1,440 team-quarters (7%), and may be mismeasured, since favorable answers can reward a likable manager, and a manager new in July 2025 is rated after one quarter. If so, I would see blanks bunched in some teams or quarters, and new managers’ ratings jumping in their first quarters. I will report the blanks and never fill them in, compare each team with itself before and after, and read the rating as the team’s view, not a measure of skill. A team compared with itself cannot separate a new manager’s first quarter from the manager’s type, so I will say so.

5. First description

Delivery (delivered_share). Kind: a measurement, a share from 0 to 1. How many: 1,440, none blank. Middle: median 0.69, and mean 0.65, which a tail of bad quarters pulls down. Spread: half fall between 0.50 and 0.83, and the range is 0 to 1. Shape: skewed left, with a long tail of quarters that delivered little (30 under 5%). Choice: each team-quarter counts once, whatever its size. Weighting by milestones gives 0.64.

Against my model: not yet able to say. The model predicts delivery rises after July 2025, by about 5 points after a first-quarter dip, and one variable can’t show whether it did. That comparison belongs in Results.

People skill (people_rating). Kind: a measurement, a share of favorable answers. How many: 1,338, with 102 blank (7%). The blank rate is the same before July 2025 as after (7.2% against 6.9%), and they are not bunched, since they come from 71 teams, at most 3 each. Middle: median 0.74, mean 0.72. Spread: half fall between 0.65 and 0.81, and the range is 0.31 to 0.94. Shape: skewed left, with a tail of low-rated team-quarters (77 below 0.50, spread over 23 teams). Choice: blanks left out, not filled in.

Against my model: not yet able to say. The model predicts higher ratings under professional managers, and one variable can’t show that.

Difficulty (hard_close). Kind: yes/No. How many: 1,440, none blank. Middle, spread and shape: 0.43 rated hard (619 quarters). With two values, the proportion says it all. Against my model: not yet able to say. The model predicts a gain on hard quarters too, and 619 hard and 821 other quarters can test that.

Note on AI use

I used Gemini (Willamette account) for the counts, middles, spreads, and histograms. I added a milestone-weighted mean, and rejected its offer to fill blank ratings, since a filled-in rating is a measurement nobody took.

Work it yourself: the Data & Methods prompts version 1

These are the prompts used to write the Data & Methods draft above, in order. Download the data, start a new Gemini chat with your Willamette account, upload the file, and paste each prompt into the same chat. Think about the question before you open “What we found.” Gemini’s wording and charts will differ from ours, but the numbers should match. If a number doesn’t, that’s a check worth running.

See exactly how we ran it Gemini's answers to these prompts, step by step (the shared chat, which opens when you sign in with your Willamette account).

P1

What is a row?

What does one row of my data represent? How many rows are there, how many different teams do they cover, and how many quarters?

Is one row the unit the model is about?

What we found

One row is one product team in one quarter, and there are 1,440 rows, 120 teams, 12 quarters (July 2023 to June 2026), 960 rows before July 2025 and 480 after. Each team has one manager at a time, so a row is also one manager’s quarter, which is what the model is about.

Check the AI’s count against something you know. Here, 120 teams times 12 quarters is 1,440. If it says anything else, find out why before you go on.

Gemini may also check, unprompted, that no team appears twice in a quarter (none does). That is the right habit. Its listing of the columns shows another useful thing, where the blanks are. people_rating has 102 (P3), esc_wait_hrs has 41, and lead_former_manager is blank for every row before July 2025, because there were no technical leads before the reorganization. The last two are in columns this version’s model does not use.

P2

Describe the outcome

Describe delivered_share: what kind of variable it is, how many values there are including blanks, the middle (the median, and the mean only if a mean makes sense for this kind of variable), how spread out it is, and its shape, with a chart. Tell me any choices you made, such as dropping blanks or zeros.

Which is larger, the mean or the median? Why?

What we found
Question Answer
Kind A measurement, a share from 0 to 1
How many 1,440, none blank
Middle Median 0.69, and mean 0.65
Spread Half fall between 0.50 and 0.83, and the range is 0 to 1
Shape Skewed left, with a long tail of quarters that delivered little (30 are under 5%)

The mean sits below the median because of that tail. A choice worth naming. Each team-quarter counts once, whatever its size. Weighting by milestones (all milestones delivered divided by all committed) gives 0.64.

Gemini will list its own choices (here, nothing dropped, 28 zeros kept, no rescaling) and may add that 43 quarters, 3%, delivered everything. (In one rerun it said 52 quarters, or 3.61%, but the file has 43, or 2.99%. A count is checkable, so ask it to show the code.) Read its list against the one above. It does not say that every team-quarter counts once, whatever its size. And it may explain the left tail as “delivery blockers or escalations” though it looked at no such column. A description of one variable can’t say why, so that explanation is a guess until you check it. (Here it happens to point the right way, since the 28 quarters that delivered nothing averaged 15.7 escalations against 9.1 overall. That is a second variable, however, and it needs its own prompt.)

P3

Describe a measurement with blanks

Describe people_rating the same way. Tell me how many are blank, and what you did with them.

Did Gemini offer to fill in the blank ratings? Would you let it?

What we found

1,338 ratings and 102 blank (7.1%). The median is 0.74 and the mean is 0.72. Half fall between 0.65 and 0.81, in a range of 0.31 to 0.94. The shape is skewed left, with a tail of low-rated team-quarters (77 below 0.50, from 23 teams).

Blanks are as common before July 2025 as after (69 of 960, 7.2%, against 33 of 480, 6.9%). The draft leaves them out and says so. A filled-in rating is a measurement nobody took, so decline the offer.

Gemini may not offer to fill them at all (it may decline on its own, and say why). Three things to read closely in its answer:

  • What the number means. The file only says people_rating, and Gemini may call it a “score” or “satisfaction.” The draft knows more. It is the share of favorable answers on the team’s upward feedback survey (see “What each column records”). A mean of a share is fine, but the meaning came from the dictionary, not the file.
  • Counts or rates? If it tabulates blanks by manager type it will say 69 engineer-managers and 33 professional, but there are 960 engineer-manager rows and 480 professional ones. Counts measure size. Rates measure performance. The rates are 7.2% and 6.9%.
  • “Tightly” and “sharply.” The ratings are not tightly clustered, since about two thirds (65%) fall between 0.65 and 0.85, and the standard deviation is 0.12. Words like these are choices too.
P4

Describe a yes/no variable

Describe hard_close the same way.

A yes/no variable has no middle or spread in the usual sense. What did Gemini report? And what did it say the column *means*?

What we found

Yes/No, 1,440 values, none blank. 619 quarters were rated hard (43%), and 821 were not. With two values the proportion says it all. Gemini may call 0.43 a “binary mean,” which is the same number, a share.

Read what it says the column means. Gemini only had the name, so it may guess, and a guess from hard_close is easy to get wrong (“a hard close protocol”). The real meaning is in the dictionary (“What each column records”). hard_close is yes when the quarter-close review rated the quarter hard for the team. Someone judged it, and when matters, which is at the close, after the outcome is known. Notice that you have not told Gemini this. The next step shows what that costs.

P5

Where could it mislead you?

My data is Fernhill Software's records, one row per product team per quarter. For each of these, say whether it could affect my data and what I would see in the data if it were happening: missing values, mismeasurement, a definition that changed, only some cases recorded, dates or entries shifted. Focus on people_rating and hard_close.

Which way is most likely to mislead you about the people-skill rating? What would you see if it were happening?

What we found

Gemini will probably go through all five for both columns and rank none. Choosing is your work. It may also run its own checks first (blanks by quarter, the rating before and after July 2025, whether any team drops out of a quarter). Read them against the file:

  • Its checks are right. Blanks run from 4 to 14 a quarter (out of 120 teams), with no quarter standing out. All 120 teams appear in all 12 quarters, and 102 ratings are blank. Its table of the rating by quarter shows no first-quarter jump for new managers, with about 0.78 in 2025Q3 and 0.79 to 0.80 after. Neither of the draft’s worries, blanks bunched or a jump in a new manager’s first quarter, is confirmed.
  • Counts again. It may report 69 engineer-manager blanks against 33 professional. With 960 and 480 rows, the rates are 7.2% and 6.9%.
  • A confident diagnosis worth doubting. The average rating steps up from 0.69 before July 2025 to 0.79 after, and its spread narrows (standard deviation 0.124 to 0.075). Gemini may call this “strong evidence” that the survey was recalibrated, a definition that changed. It might be. But the step lands exactly where the managers changed, which is what the model predicts, with new managers, hired on people skill, rated by their teams. This file cannot tell “the survey changed” from “the managers changed.” The next step is a question for the people who produce the data. Did the survey change in July 2025? Until you know, the honest sentence is “can’t tell yet.”
  • What did it take hard_close to mean? Its paragraphs on hard_close treat the column as a governance flag (“a soft close,” “criteria for declaring a hard close”). They are built on a guess, and the cost shows. What it says to look for is not what could go wrong with a rating made after the outcome.

The draft picks the rating, which may be missing and mismeasured, since favorable answers can reward a likable manager, and a manager new in July 2025 is rated after only one quarter. If that were happening you would see blanks bunched in some teams or quarters, and new managers’ ratings jumping in their first quarters. It leaves the step at July 2025 for the Results draft, where ratings rising is one of the model’s predictions. Either pick can be defended. What you owe the reader is one choice, what you would see if it were happening, and what you will do.

Correction: hard_close is not a protocol. In this file it is "yes" when the quarter-close review rated the quarter as hard for the team, a judgment made at the end of the quarter, after the outcome is known. Knowing that, what should I keep in mind whenever I use hard_close?

Does Gemini notice that the rating is made after the result is known? What could that do to a comparison of hard and easy quarters?

What we found

A good answer notices the hindsight problem. A quarter that went badly may get called hard because it went badly, so “hard quarters delivered less” can be partly circular. If Gemini doesn’t get there on its own, say so, and say it yourself. Give your AI the dictionary at the start, not after it has guessed. The same went for the people-skill rating in P3, where the guess (“satisfaction”) was closer but still a guess.

Gemini may go further and check against the data without being asked (a good sign). Quarters rated hard average a 48.9% delivery share and 13.8 escalations, against 76.5% and 5.6 for the rest (correlations −0.57 with delivery and +0.61 with escalations). Those numbers are right. Read its conclusions more carefully than its numbers. It may declare that hard_close is “an effect, not a cause” and that bad results “drive the rating, not the other way around.” The file shows an association, not a direction. A quarter can be genuinely harder, and also be called hard because it went badly, and both are plausible. A description can’t separate them. Notice also its advice never to use the column at all. For a version of this project with no other measure of difficulty, the honest course is to use it and say what it can’t tell you.

P6

Hold it up against the prediction

My model predicts that delivery rises about 5 points after July 2025, that people-skill ratings rise, and that the rise holds on hard quarters as well as easy ones. Based only on the descriptions above, does the data look the way the model says it should? What can a description of one variable at a time not tell me?

What would you write for each of the three predictions, using only what you have described so far?

What we found

From the descriptions alone, not yet able to say, for all three. Each description is of one variable at a time, and none can show whether delivery rose after July 2025, or whether the rise holds on hard quarters. “Not yet able to say” is an honest sentence, and a better one than a confident sentence you can’t back.

Gemini will probably not stop there. Asked to use “only the descriptions above,” it may go back to the file and run the comparisons itself (“based on the full dataset”). Credit the numbers, and notice the instruction it set aside. The numbers are right, and they are the Results draft arriving early.

What it may report Value
Average delivery, before and after July 2025 65.3% then 63.4% (1.9 points lower)
Median delivery, before and after 68.2% then 72.6% (about 4 points higher)
Average rating, before and after 0.69 then 0.79
Easy quarters, before and after 74.9% then 79.4%
Hard quarters, before and after 52.8% then 41.0%

Three things to read closely:

  • The mean and the median disagree. The average fell and the middle quarter rose, because the spread widened. The lower quarter of team-quarters fell (the lowest tenth from 35% to 19%), while the upper half rose (the median from 68% to 73%, and the top quartile’s edge from 82% to 85%). Which summary you pick changes the headline, and you should say which you used. Gemini offered both, and the Results draft compares averages.
  • It splits by hard_close with no caution. Two prompts earlier it warned that the rating is made after the outcome. Here it says the third prediction “does not hold” on the strength of that split, without repeating the warning. A quarter that went badly gets called hard, so part of “hard quarters fell” is circular. The AI forgot its own advice, and you can’t.
  • Its second answer is the useful one. A single variable can’t show a change over time, an interaction between two variables, a correlation, or a shift in who is in the group. That is exactly what Module 2 is for.

Results draft version 1

Download the PDF The same draft as a three-page document, with its charts. It runs long on purpose, as its note on length explains.

1. The question and the prediction

My question is causal. Would replacing engineer-managers with professional managers, technical leads and AI raise delivery (the share of a team’s committed milestones delivered by their dates)? A before-and-after can answer only a descriptive question, so that is this draft’s question. How did delivery and people-skill ratings move from the eight quarters before July 2025 to the four after? My model predicts delivery up about 5 points after a first-quarter dip, ratings up, and the rise holding on hard quarters.

2. The charts

The first chart plots every team in every quarter as a faint dot and draws the median, the average and the 25th and 75th percentiles through them, with a dashed line where the reorganization began.

This chart answers: how did delivery move, quarter by quarter, before and after the reorganization?

Delivery is a measurement (a share), and the quarter is a date. Each dot is one team in one quarter, 120 a quarter. The solid line joins the quarterly medians and the dashed line joins the quarterly averages. The dotted lines join the 25th and 75th percentiles, with a quarter of teams below the first and a quarter above the second.

The quarters are noisy, so the second chart pools them into before and after, stacks the two on one shared axis, and marks the average and the median on each.

This chart answers: how is delivery spread across team-quarters before and after July 2025, and where do the average, the median and the most common band fall?

Delivery is a measurement (a share). Each bar is the share of that period’s team-quarters in a ten-point band (960 before, 480 after). The dashed line marks the average, the solid line marks the median, and the darkest bar marks the most common band.

Delivery was not the only record that moved in July 2025, and the third chart shows what else did.

This chart answers: what else changed in July 2025?

Each panel is one record averaged over the 120 teams each quarter. The panels show the share with a professional manager (labels), the share with AI licenses (yes/no), and milestones committed per team (counts).

3. The association

On average, delivery is lower after July 2025, at 63.4% against 65.3% before, a difference of 1.9 points. This is measured at the team-quarter level, over 1,440 team-quarters (960 before, 480 after). But the middle moved the other way. The median team-quarter delivered 72.6% after against 68.2% before, which is 4.4 points higher. The most common band (80% to 90%, by a hair before) did not move at all.

The three measures disagree because they answer different questions, and they agree only when a distribution is symmetric. The average is the balance point, the median is the middle, and the most common band is the peak. This distribution is skewed left, with a long tail of weak quarters, and the tail got longer. The weakest tenth of team-quarters delivered about 35% or less before and about 19% or less after, so the average follows the tail while the median follows the middle.

At the average, the fall is weak. Every after-quarter (61.4% to 67.8%) sits inside the range of the before-quarters (61.4% to 70.3%), which moved about 3 points from one quarter to the next. At the team level, the fall holds, barely. Of 120 teams, 68 delivered less after, and the median team fell 2.7 points. This is the middle of the team changes, not the change in the middle. Without the first after-quarter, the fall is 1.2 points, and weighted by milestones it is 1.3 points. At the team level, however, 56 of 120 teams delivered less without that quarter, and the median team’s change is +1.0 point, so “lower” leans on one quarter.

Split by the quarter-close rating, quarters rated easy rose from 74.9% to 79.4%, and quarters rated hard fell from 52.8% to 41.0%. People-skill ratings rose from 0.69 to 0.79 (1,338 ratings, with 102 blank and left out).

And the two changes are one variable. In all 1,440 team-quarters a professional manager and AI licenses go together, 480 with both and 960 with neither. The third chart’s first two panels are the same line.

4. Against the model

I can’t tell yet on delivery, because the summaries disagree. The average is not higher, but the median is (4.4 points, near the 5 predicted). Ratings rose while the average didn’t, which is the model’s second test, and hard quarters fell, which is its third.

But I can’t tell whether the model failed or the comparison did. With the reorganization and AI arriving together, any difference belongs to both, and nothing in this file can split it.

5. What this does not establish

The strongest other explanation is a change at the same moment, the year’s customer migration. If it lowered delivery, I would expect more work committed after July 2025 in every team, and a smaller share delivered even where more was delivered. Committed milestones rose from 18.0 to 20.2 per team-quarter (12%), and delivered milestones rose from 11.6 to 12.8 while the share fell.

The hard-quarter split is partly circular. Difficulty is rated at close, after the outcome, and quarters that delivered under 60% were rated hard 83% of the time, against 21% of the rest.

My Data & Methods concern, the ratings, changes little here, since blanks are 7% before and after, though a manager rated after one quarter may enjoy a honeymoon. Noticed, not pursued. Escalations fell from 9.9 to 7.5 a team-quarter, and lead departures rose from 3.6% to 11.9% a quarter.

The decision needs a model that explains. Fernhill must choose what to keep, and a forecast for the package can’t say which part delivered what, or why the weakest quarters got weaker while the middle improved.

What would separate the changes, using records Fernhill already keeps:

  • Give the changes to different teams by lot, since AI licenses arrive in waves anyway. Some teams keep an engineer-manager without AI for a year, some get AI only, and some get the reorganization with AI.
  • Set each group against its own eight quarters before, which the planning tool already holds, so the migration falls on every group alike.
  • Rate difficulty at the quarterly planning review, before the work, instead of at close.
  • Follow escalations and waits in the issue tracker, where the technical questions the model leaves to AI and the lead actually go.

Note on AI use

I used Gemini (Willamette account) for the averages and medians, the team-level changes, the crosstab, and the charts. It called the before-and-after difference “the effect of the reorganization.” I changed that to “lower after July 2025,” since nothing here separates the reorganization from AI or the migration. It gave the average alone. I added the median and the most common band, which tell a different story.

A note on length

This draft runs over the limit on purpose. It is longer than two pages and has three charts, where the rubric asks for one to two pages and one or two charts. The second chart is there to show that the average, the median and the most common band tell different stories, which is the point of section 3, and I would rather make that point than keep to the limit. Under the rubric that costs the draft something, and I accept the cost.

Work it yourself: the Results prompts version 1

These are the prompts used to write the Results draft above, in order, in the same chat as the Data & Methods prompts (or a new one with the data uploaded again). Think about the question before you open “What we found.” Gemini’s charts and wording will differ from ours, but the numbers should match. If a number doesn’t, that’s a check worth running.

See exactly how we ran it Gemini's answers to these prompts, step by step (the shared chat, which opens when you sign in with your Willamette account).

P7

A chart for a question

Chart the average delivered_share for each quarter, over all teams, as a line, with a vertical line where July 2025 starts. Tell me what one dot represents.

Is one dot a team, a quarter, or a team-quarter?

What we found

Each dot is one quarter’s average over all 120 teams, which gives 12 dots. Before July 2025 they run 70.3, 66.7, 65.5, 63.2, 68.0, 64.3, 61.4, and 62.8. After, they run 61.4, 61.7, 67.8, and 62.6. Every after-quarter (61.4 to 67.8) sits inside the range of the before-quarters (61.4 to 70.3), which moved about 3 points from one quarter to the next. Before you ask for a chart, say what one dot should be. It is Module 1’s “what is a row?” again.

P8

Average, median and most common value

Show the distribution of delivered_share before July 2025 and after as two histograms with ten-point bands on the same scale. Mark the average and the median on each, and tell me which band is most common in each. Tell me what one bar represents.

The average and the median may not move the same way. What does each one tell you, and when would they be the same?

What we found
Before July 2025 After July 2025
Average 65.3% 63.4%
Median 68.2% 72.6%
Most common band (bands include their lower edge) 80% to 90% 80% to 90%
Spread (standard deviation) 0.217 0.275

Three measures, three stories. The average fell 1.9 points, the median rose 4.4, and the most common band did not move (see below). They are not the same thing. The average is the balance point, pulled by every value including the extremes. The median is the middle, which ignores how far the tails go. The most common band is the peak. They agree only when a distribution is symmetric, and this one is skewed left. After July 2025 the tail got heavier, as the share of team-quarters delivering under 10% went from 1.2% to 6.7%, while the middle and the top rose. The average followed the tail, and the median followed the middle. Which one to report depends on the question, and you owe the reader both and a reason. One bar is the share of that period’s team-quarters in a ten-point band (use shares, not counts, since there are 960 before and 480 after).

P9

The comparison, and the row counts

Compare the average delivered_share before July 2025 with the average after, over all team-quarters, and give the median too. Show the number of rows in each period.

Would you write that the reorganization lowered delivery?

What we found
Rows Average Median
Before July 2025 960 65.3% 68.2%
After July 2025 480 63.4% 72.6%

The average is 1.9 points lower after, and the median is 4.4 points higher. That is a description, and it already shows why P8 matters. Notice there are twice as many rows before as after, and that the average’s difference is small next to the 3 points the quarters already move on their own. The draft writes “lower after July 2025 on average,” not “the effect of the reorganization,” and so should you.

P10

Does it hold up?

For each team, compare its average delivered_share before July 2025 with its average after. How many teams delivered less after, and what is the median change? Then repeat the comparison of all team-quarters leaving out 2025Q3, and again weighting each team-quarter by milestones_committed.

Is "lower" robust, or does it depend on how you count?

What we found

68 of 120 teams delivered less after, and the median team fell 2.7 points. Without 2025Q3, the first quarter after, the team-quarter average falls 1.2 points, and weighted by milestones, over all quarters, it falls 1.3 points. The direction of the average survives both ways of counting, and it stays small. It does not survive for the typical team. Gemini also redid the team comparison without 2025Q3 when we ran it. 56 of 120 teams delivered less, and the median team’s change was +1.0 point. “Lower” leans on one quarter. If a number differs slightly, check how Gemini rounded before you worry.

P11

Split by difficulty

Compare the average delivered_share before and after July 2025 separately for quarters rated hard (hard_close = yes) and quarters rated easy. Show the number of rows in each group.

Can you trust this split? Who rated the quarters hard, and when?

What we found
Before After
Rated easy 74.9% (541 rows) 79.4% (280 rows)
Rated hard 52.8% (419 rows) 41.0% (200 rows)

Easy quarters rose and hard quarters fell. But difficulty is rated at the close, after the outcome. Quarters that delivered under 60% were rated hard 83% of the time, against 21% of the rest. Part of this split is circular, because a quarter that went badly gets called hard. The model’s third prediction can’t be tested cleanly with this column.

P12

The people-skill ratings

Compare the average people_rating before and after July 2025, leaving out the blanks. Show how many ratings are in each period.

Which of the model's predictions does this support?

What we found

Ratings rose from 0.69 to 0.79 (891 ratings before and 447 after, with the 102 blanks left out). That supports the model’s second prediction, and it sits next to a delivery figure that did not rise. If people skill drove delivery, both should have moved. Ratings up while delivery isn’t is a result, not a failure.

P13

What else changed in July 2025?

Cross-tabulate manager_type by ai_access, with the counts. Then show, for each period, the average milestones_committed and milestones_delivered per team-quarter.

If two changes arrive together, what can this file say about either one?

What we found
No AI licenses AI licenses
Engineer-manager 960 0
Professional manager 0 480

Every professional manager comes with AI, and every engineer-manager without. The two changes are one variable, with 480 team-quarters with both, 960 with neither, and nothing with one but not the other. No analysis of this file can separate them. And a third thing changed. Committed milestones rose from 18.0 to 20.2 per team-quarter (12%) and delivered milestones from 11.6 to 12.8, so a smaller share of a larger load was delivered. That is the year’s customer migration, a rival explanation.

P14

What did you notice but not pursue?

Compare the average escalations per team-quarter, and the share of team-quarters with lead_departed = yes, before and after July 2025.

Neither is in the model. Which would you chase first, and why?

What we found

Escalations fell from 9.9 to 7.5 per team-quarter, and lead departures rose from 3.6% to 11.9% a quarter (35 departures in the eight quarters before, 57 in the four after). The model doesn’t mention either. The draft records them as noticed but not pursued, and what to do about them is the question the next version has to answer.
